title: German expansion and the international response (1933–1940)
summary: Hitler's step-by-step overturning of Versailles, the policy of appeasement, the Nazi–Soviet Pact and the outbreak of war, plus the historians' debate over Hitler's intentions.

keyterms.definition: 'Living space': Hitler's aim of conquering land in eastern Europe for German settlement and resources.
March 1936 entry of German troops into the demilitarised zone west of the Rhine, breaking Versailles and Locarno without resistance.
Union of Germany and Austria, forbidden by Versailles, carried out by German troops in March 1938.
British and French policy of meeting reasonable German grievances through negotiation and concession to avoid war, associated with Neville Chamberlain.
September 1938 agreement of Germany, Britain, France and Italy to transfer the Sudetenland from Czechoslovakia to Germany; Czechoslovakia was not consulted.
Border regions of Czechoslovakia with about three million ethnic Germans and key fortifications.
August 1939 non-aggression pact between Germany and the USSR with a secret protocol dividing Poland and eastern Europe into spheres.
Record of a November 1937 meeting where Hitler told military leaders of plans to seize Austria and Czechoslovakia; used by historians debating his intentions.
'Lightning war': rapid attacks combining tanks, motorised infantry and aircraft, as used against Poland (1939) and France (1940).
Interpretation that Hitler followed a long-held plan for expansion, as argued by Hugh Trevor-Roper.
A.J.P. Taylor's 1961 argument that Hitler was an opportunist who exploited others' mistakes rather than following a blueprint.

questions.prompt: Put these German actions in chronological order.
items: Germany leaves the League of Nations
questions.explanation: October 1933, January 1935, March 1935, March 1936, March 1938.

questions.prompt: Why did the Anglo-German Naval Agreement (June 1935) weaken the Stresa Front?
options: Britain approved German naval rearmament without consulting France or Italy
It handed Germany Britain's colonies
It forbade Germany to build submarines
It made Germany a member of the Stresa Front
questions.explanation: Allowing Germany a fleet of 35% of British surface tonnage condoned a breach of Versailles only weeks after Stresa.

questions.statement: France sent troops to resist the remilitarisation of the Rhineland in 1936.
questions.explanation: France, in an election campaign and unwilling to act without Britain, protested but did nothing; Britain saw Germany as entering its 'own back garden'.

questions.text: Hitler's aim of gaining land in the east for German settlement was called ___.
questions.explanation: Lebensraum was set out in Mein Kampf and pointed towards war with Poland and the USSR.

questions.prompt: What did the 1935 Saar plebiscite show?
options: About 90% of voters chose to return to Germany
The Saar voted to join France
The League refused to hold a vote
Voters chose to stay under League rule by a large margin
questions.explanation: The League-run vote was a propaganda triumph that Hitler presented as proof of German national unity.

questions.prompt: Match each person to their role.

pairs.right: French PM who signed at Munich

questions.explanation: Schuschnigg's call for a plebiscite on independence prompted Hitler to invade Austria in March 1938.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT usually given as a reason for British appeasement?
options: Fear of bombing of cities
Belief that Versailles had treated Germany harshly
Britain's military superiority made war unnecessary
Need for time to rearm
questions.explanation: Chamberlain's government believed Britain was NOT ready for war; rearmament, public opinion, the empire and the economy all encouraged negotiation.

questions.statement: The Hossbach Memorandum recorded Hitler discussing plans to take Austria and Czechoslovakia.
questions.explanation: It was used at Nuremberg as evidence of planning; Taylor argued it was a daydream rather than a blueprint.

questions.text: Union between Germany and Austria was called the ___.
questions.explanation: It was forbidden by Versailles and Saint-Germain, but a rigged plebiscite in April 1938 claimed over 99% approval.

questions.prompt: How did Mussolini respond to the Anschluss in 1938?
options: He accepted it, unlike his reaction in 1934
He mobilised troops on the Brenner Pass
He declared war on Germany
He referred it to the League
questions.explanation: By 1938 Italy was tied to Germany through the Axis; Hitler promised never to forget Mussolini's acceptance.

questions.prompt: Which country was NOT represented at the Munich Conference in September 1938?
options: Italy
Czechoslovakia
France
Britain
questions.explanation: Czechoslovakia and the USSR were excluded; the Czechs were told to accept or fight alone.

questions.text: The Munich Agreement transferred the ___ to Germany.
questions.explanation: Losing the Sudeten fortifications left the rest of Czechoslovakia defenceless.

questions.prompt: Put these events of 1938–39 in chronological order.
questions.explanation: 30 September 1938, 15 March 1939, 31 March 1939, 23 August 1939, 1 September 1939.

questions.prompt: Why is the occupation of Prague in March 1939 seen as a turning point?
options: It was Hitler's first seizure of non-German people, discrediting the self-determination argument
It ended the Spanish Civil War
It led directly to the Anschluss
It was approved by the League
questions.explanation: Appeasement rested partly on the idea that Hitler only wanted Germans; Prague showed otherwise and Britain guaranteed Poland.

questions.statement: The Nazi–Soviet Pact included a secret protocol dividing Poland between Germany and the USSR.
questions.explanation: The protocol also assigned the Baltic states and Bessarabia to Soviet influence; the USSR invaded eastern Poland on 17 September 1939.

questions.prompt: Why did Stalin agree to the Nazi–Soviet Pact?
options: He trusted Hitler completely
He doubted Western commitment after Munich and wanted time and territory
Britain had asked him to sign it
The League ordered it
questions.explanation: Slow, half-hearted Anglo-French talks in Moscow and exclusion from Munich convinced Stalin to buy time and a buffer zone.

questions.prompt: Match each historian to their view.

pairs.right: Hitler was an opportunist, not a planner
Hitler followed long-term aims from Mein Kampf
Appeasers were weak and to blame
Chamberlain had alternatives but chose appeasement

questions.explanation: Interpretations range from blaming the 'guilty men' to revisionist sympathy for the constraints Chamberlain faced.

questions.text: Britain and France declared war on Germany on 3 September ___.
questions.explanation: Germany ignored their ultimatum to withdraw from Poland, which it had invaded on 1 September.

questions.statement: Britain and France launched a major offensive into Germany in autumn 1939 to save Poland.
questions.explanation: Apart from a limited French probe into the Saar, the West did not attack; this lull became known as the 'Phoney War'.

options: Germany invaded the USSR
Germany defeated France and the Low Countries using Blitzkrieg tactics
Britain signed an armistice with Germany
Italy surrendered
questions.explanation: Germany attacked on 10 May; France signed an armistice on 22 June 1940 after British troops were evacuated from Dunkirk.
